hints.content: A pair of figures is similar if we can map one onto the other using only rigid transformations and dilations.

Some rectangles are similar to each other. For example, you can map the smaller rectangle below onto the larger rectangle by dilating it by a factor of $2$ about point $P$.


[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: Two rectangles in the first quadrant of a coordinate plane. The first rectangle will have points at three, two, three, five, seven, two, and seven, four. There is a point P at the center at five, three. The second rectangle has points at one, one, one, five, nine, one,  and nine, five. All angles are ninety degrees.

hints.content:
Some rectangles are not similar to each other. For example, you can't map rectangle $ABCD$ onto rectangle $ABEF$ using rigid transformations and dilations alone. In order to map $ABCD$ onto $ABEF$ you must increase its height without changing its width. A dilation can only change both dimensions.



[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: Two rectangles A B C D and A B E F in the first quadrant of a coordinate plane. The first rectangle has point A at one, five, point B is at five, five, point C is at five, two, and point D is at one, two. The second rectangle has point A at one, five, point B is at five, five, point E is at five, one, and point F is at one, one.

hints.content: In conclusion, a rectangle is **sometimes** similar to another rectangle, because we can **sometimes** map one onto the other using only dilations and rigid transformations.
